title: Gender-specific mortality in DTP-IPV- and MMR±MenC-eligible age groups to determine possible sex-differential effects of vaccination: an observational study.
ehr_evidence: The data were available from Statistics Netherlands, who linked demographic data of persons included in the Municipal Personal Records Database (GBA) with causes of death derived from Statistics Netherlands.
summary: A large national observational cohort study of all Dutch children aged 0-11 years (2000-2011) comparing gender-specific mortality rates across age groups defined by the last scheduled vaccine received.
key_findings: During the study period, 14,038 children (0.22%) died, 91% attributed to a known natural cause of death.
The mortality rate for natural causes was higher among boys than girls in all age groups.
Adjusted IRRs for girls compared with boys ranged between 0.81 (95% CI 0.74-0.89) and 0.91 (95% CI 0.77-1.07) across age groups.

No significant difference in IRR was observed between all vaccine-related age groups (p = 0.723), between children 2-13 months (following DTP-IPV) and 14 months-3 years (following MMR±MenC) (p = 0.493), or between children 14 months-3 years and 4-8 years (p = 0.868).

Sensitivity analyses (indigenous Dutch children only, before/after September 2002, excluding perinatal/congenital causes, infectious/parasitic diseases only) showed no significant differences in IRR between vaccine-related age groups.
population: All Dutch children aged 0-11 years, born/living in the Netherlands 2000-2011 (N = 6,261,472)
limitations: Individual vaccination status could not be verified; the study assumed all children were vaccinated according to the national schedule, which may have underestimated the effect of the last received vaccine.
Very low childhood mortality in this high-income setting limits statistical power to detect non-specific sex-differential effects.
Changes in the vaccination schedule during the study period and possible interference from BCG vaccination.
Assumption of complete adherence to schedule may introduce selection/survival bias.
data_availability_statement: We thank Statistics Netherlands, who have made the data available and made it possible to link demographic data of persons included in the Municipal Personal Records Database (GBA) with causes of death.
